notes.definition: Soluble salts can be made by reacting an acid with a solid insoluble substance such as a metal, metal oxide, metal hydroxide or metal carbonate. The solid is added until no more reacts, the excess is filtered off, and the salt solution is crystallised to give the solid salt.
explanation: A soluble salt is a salt that dissolves in water, such as copper sulfate, zinc chloride or magnesium sulfate. To make one, choose an acid that provides the negative ion you want (hydrochloric acid for a chloride, nitric acid for a nitrate, sulfuric acid for a sulfate) and an insoluble solid that contains the metal you want. The solid can be the metal itself (if it reacts with acids, such as magnesium or zinc), its oxide, its hydroxide or its carbonate.

The key idea is to add the insoluble solid in excess. The solid is added to the acid a little at a time, with stirring, until no more reacts and some solid is left over. With a carbonate or metal you know the reaction has finished because fizzing stops; with an oxide or hydroxide the solid simply stops disappearing. Adding excess solid makes sure that all of the acid has reacted, so the salt solution is not contaminated with acid. Because the solid is insoluble, the excess can then be removed easily by filtration.

Required practical 1 is to make a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt, for example copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l). Warm the acid gently (to about 50 °C, using a water bath or a low Bunsen flame, without boiling) to speed up the reaction. Add black copper oxide powder a spatula at a time and stir until some black solid remains. Filter the mixture into an evaporating basin: the excess copper oxide stays on the filter paper and the blue copper sulfate solution (the filtrate) passes through.

To get crystals, heat the filtrate gently in the evaporating basin over a water bath (or with a low flame) to evaporate some of the water, until the solution reaches its crystallisation point. You can check this by dipping in a cold glass rod: if small crystals form on it, stop heating. Leave the solution to cool slowly, so that crystals form as the salt becomes less soluble. Filter or pour off any remaining solution, then pat the crystals dry between filter papers or leave them in a warm place. Heating the solution to dryness is avoided because the salt can spit and the crystals can be damaged or decompose.

Safety matters in this practical. Wear eye protection, because dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant and hot solutions can spit. Copper oxide and copper sulfate are harmful, so avoid skin contact and wash hands afterwards. Do not boil the acid, and take care with hot apparatus. You may be asked to plan how to make a different named salt from information provided, for example zinc sulfate from zinc carbonate and sulfuric acid, or magnesium chloride from magnesium oxide and hydrochloric acid: the same steps apply.
keyFacts: Soluble salts are made by reacting an acid with an insoluble metal, metal oxide, metal hydroxide or metal carbonate.
The solid is added in excess until no more reacts, so that all the acid is used up.
The excess solid is removed by filtration.
The salt solution is crystallised by evaporating some water, then leaving it to cool.
Copper sulfate: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l); black solid dissolves to give a blue solution.
The acid is warmed (not boiled) to speed up the reaction.
Heat on a water bath to the crystallisation point; do not heat to dryness.
Dry the crystals by patting them with filter paper or leaving them in a warm place.
With a carbonate or metal, fizzing stops when the acid has all reacted.

keyTerms.definition: A salt that dissolves in water, such as copper sulfate or zinc chloride.
More of a reactant than is needed to react completely with the other reactant, so some is left over.
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper; the solid stays on the paper and the liquid (filtrate) passes through.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper; here, the salt solution.
The solid left on the filter paper; here, the excess insoluble solid.
Forming solid crystals from a solution by evaporating some of the solvent and allowing the solution to cool.
The point at which the solution is concentrated enough for crystals to start forming as it cools.

workedExamples.title: Choosing reactants for a named salt
workedExamples.question: Suggest reactants to make zinc sulfate crystals, and explain why zinc carbonate is a good choice of solid.
steps: The salt is a sulfate, so use dilute sulfuric acid.
The metal is zinc, so use an insoluble zinc compound: zinc oxide, zinc hydroxide, zinc carbonate or zinc metal.
Zinc carbonate is insoluble, so excess can be filtered off.
It fizzes as it reacts, so you can see when the reaction has stopped (fizzing stops with solid left over).
workedExamples.answer: Dilute sulfuric acid and zinc carbonate (in excess). Fizzing stopping shows all the acid has reacted.

workedExamples.title: Processing results: mass of excess reactant
workedExamples.question: A student added 3.0 g of copper oxide to warm sulfuric acid. After filtering, the dried excess copper oxide had a mass of 0.6 g. Calculate the mass of copper oxide that reacted.
steps: Mass reacted = mass added − mass left over.

workedExamples.title: Mass of salt from a known mass of oxide
workedExamples.question: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. 79.5 g of copper oxide makes 159.5 g of copper sulfate. Calculate the maximum mass of copper sulfate made from 2.4 g of copper oxide.
steps: The ratio of masses is fixed: mass of CuSO₄ = 2.4 × 159.5 ÷ 79.5.
= 4.815 g, which is 4.82 g to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the acid should be added in excess so that all the solid dissolves.
misconceptions.right: The insoluble solid is added in excess. Any unreacted solid can be filtered off, but excess acid would stay in the solution and contaminate the salt.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the salt is caught on the filter paper.
misconceptions.right: The salt is dissolved, so it passes through the filter paper in the filtrate. The filter paper holds back the excess insoluble solid.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think you should boil the solution until all the water has gone.
misconceptions.right: Heat gently only until the crystallisation point, then let it cool. Heating to dryness can make the salt spit and can damage the crystals, giving a powder instead of crystals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think copper metal can be used to make copper sulfate with dilute sulfuric acid.
misconceptions.right: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react with dilute acids, so copper oxide, hydroxide or carbonate is used instead.

realWorld: Copper sulfate is used as a fungicide on crops and to stop algae growing in ponds.
Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salts) is used in bath salts and as a fertiliser to supply magnesium to plants.
Zinc sulfate is added to some animal feeds and dietary supplements as a source of zinc.
The chemical industry uses the same steps (react, filter, crystallise, dry) on a much larger scale to make pure salts.
examTips: Learn the method as four key steps: react (with excess solid), filter, crystallise, dry.
Always explain why the solid is added in excess: to make sure all the acid has reacted.
Name the substance on the filter paper (excess copper oxide) and in the filtrate (copper sulfate solution).
When asked how you know the solid is in excess, say 'solid stops disappearing and some is left' or, for a carbonate, 'fizzing stops'.
For a 6-mark method, give measurements (e.g. 40 cm³ of acid, warm to about 50 °C) and safety (eye protection, do not boil).
summary: Soluble salts are made from an acid and an insoluble metal, oxide, hydroxide or carbonate.
Add the solid in excess so that all the acid reacts.
Filter to remove the excess solid; the salt solution is the filtrate.
Evaporate gently to the crystallisation point, then cool to form crystals.
Dry the crystals with filter paper or in a warm place.
Copper sulfate: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O (black solid → blue solution).

flashcards.front: Which types of insoluble solid can react with an acid to make a soluble salt?
flashcards.back: Metals (above hydrogen), metal oxides, metal hydroxides and metal carbonates.

flashcards.front: Why is the insoluble solid added in excess?
flashcards.back: To make sure all the acid has reacted, so the salt is not contaminated with acid.

flashcards.front: How is the excess solid removed?
How do you know an oxide is in excess?
flashcards.back: No more dissolves and some solid is left in the beaker.

flashcards.front: How do you know a carbonate is in excess?
flashcards.back: Fizzing stops and some solid is left over.

flashcards.front: Equation for making copper sulfate from copper oxide

flashcards.back: When the solution is concentrated enough that crystals start to form (e.g. on a cold glass rod) as it cools.

flashcards.front: Why not heat the salt solution to dryness?
flashcards.back: It may spit, and the crystals could be damaged or decompose; you get small crystals or powder.
Pat dry between filter papers, or leave in a warm place (or a desiccator).

flashcards.front: What colour is copper sulfate solution?

flashcards.back: Dilute hydrochloric acid and an insoluble magnesium compound (or magnesium metal), such as magnesium oxide or carbonate, in excess.

questions.question: When making copper sulfate, why is copper oxide added to the sulfuric acid until it is in excess?
options: To make sure all the acid reacts
To make the solution turn blue faster
To stop the copper oxide being filtered
markScheme: 1 mark: to make sure all the acid reacts / is used up
questions.explanation: Excess solid means there is no acid left in the salt solution. The excess solid can be filtered off because it is insoluble.

questions.question: Which method is used to remove excess copper oxide from copper sulfate solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: filtration
questions.explanation: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a solution. Evaporation is used later to remove water from the solution.

questions.question: A student adds black copper oxide powder to warm sulfuric acid. How can she tell that the copper oxide is in excess?
options: Black solid remains and no more dissolves
markScheme: 1 mark: black solid remains / no more dissolves
questions.explanation: When all the acid has reacted, extra copper oxide stays undissolved. Copper oxide does not fizz with acid (no gas is made), and the solution turns blue, not colourless.

questions.question: Which reactants could be used to make crystals of zinc chloride by adding an insoluble solid to an acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: zinc carbonate and hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Chloride comes from hydrochloric acid; zinc comes from insoluble zinc carbonate. Sulfuric and nitric acids would make zinc sulfate and zinc nitrate.

questions.question: Why is the sulfuric acid warmed before the copper oxide is added?
options: To make the acid more concentrated
To make the copper oxide soluble in water
markScheme: 1 mark: to speed up the reaction / increase the rate
questions.explanation: Particles move faster at higher temperatures, so the reaction is faster. The acid is warmed, not boiled, for safety.

options: Boiling would turn the copper sulfate back into copper oxide and acid
A water bath heats it gently, so the solution does not spit and the crystals are not damaged
A water bath adds water to the crystals
Boiling would make the solution acidic
markScheme: 1 mark: gentle heating stops spitting / prevents the crystals being damaged (decomposing)
questions.explanation: Gentle heating to the crystallisation point, then slow cooling, gives good crystals safely. Heating to dryness can make the hot salt spit and can damage the crystals.

questions.question: A student makes copper sulfate using copper carbonate instead of copper oxide. How can he tell when the acid has all reacted?
options: Fizzing stops and some green solid is left over
markScheme: 1 mark: fizzing stops and solid is left over
questions.explanation: Carbonates fizz with acid because carbon dioxide is produced. When the acid is used up, the fizzing stops and the excess carbonate (green) remains.

questions.question: What colour is the filtrate when copper sulfate is made from copper oxide and sulfuric acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: blue
questions.explanation: Copper sulfate solution is blue. The black copper oxide stays on the filter paper.

questions.question: Which of these could not be used with dilute sulfuric acid to make copper sulfate?
markScheme: 1 mark: copper metal
questions.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids. The oxide, hydroxide and carbonate all neutralise the acid.

questions.question: A student makes magnesium sulfate from magnesium oxide and sulfuric acid. Which is the correct order of steps?
options: Filter, add excess magnesium oxide, evaporate, cool
Add excess magnesium oxide, evaporate, filter, cool
Add excess magnesium oxide, filter, evaporate, cool
Evaporate the acid, add magnesium oxide, filter, cool
markScheme: 1 mark: add excess magnesium oxide, filter, evaporate, cool
questions.explanation: The excess solid must be filtered off before evaporating, otherwise it would end up mixed with the crystals. Crystals form when the concentrated solution cools.

questions.question:
A student added copper oxide to some warm sulfuric acid.
The student filtered off the excess copper oxide, then dried and weighed it.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mass of copper oxide that reacted.
questions.explanation: Mass reacted = mass added − mass left over = 3.0 − 0.6 = 2.4 g.

questions.question:
A student made crystals of a salt in an evaporating basin.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the mass of crystals.
questions.explanation: Subtract the mass of the empty basin: 51.40 − 48.25 = 3.15 g.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Mg = 24; S = 32; O = 16
questions.explanation: Magnesium 24, sulfur 32 and four oxygens 4 × 16 = 64. Total 24 + 32 + 64 = 120.

questions.question:
Copper oxide reacts with sulfuric acid.
CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O
Table 1 shows the mass of copper sulfate produced from 79.5 g of copper oxide.
Calculate the maximum mass of copper sulfate that can be made from 2.4 g of copper oxide.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

headers: Mass of copper oxide in g
Mass of copper sulfate produced in g

questions.explanation: The masses are in a fixed ratio: 159.5 ÷ 79.5 = 2.006, and 2.4 × 2.006 = 4.815 g, which is 4.82 g to 3 significant figures.

questions.question:
Calculate the percentage by mass of copper in copper sulfate, CuSO₄.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Cu = 63.5; S = 32; O = 16
markScheme: 1 mark: Mr of CuSO₄ = 63.5 + 32 + 64 = 159.5

questions.question:
Copper oxide reacts with sulfuric acid.
Name the salt produced.
Write the word equation for the reaction.
acceptedAnswers: copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water
markScheme: 1 mark: copper sulfate
1 mark: copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water
questions.explanation: Acid + base (metal oxide) → salt + water. Sulfuric acid makes sulfates.

questions.question: Name the process used to obtain solid salt crystals from a salt solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: crystallisation
questions.explanation: Some water is evaporated to concentrate the solution, and crystals form as it cools.

questions.question:
A student makes copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide and sulfuric acid.
Give one hazard in this experiment.
Give a precaution to reduce the risk from this hazard.
markScheme: 1 mark: hazard, e.g. sulfuric acid is an irritant / hot solution may spit / copper sulfate or copper oxide is harmful
1 mark: matching precaution, e.g. wear eye protection / heat gently and do not boil / avoid skin contact and wash hands
questions.explanation: The precaution must match the hazard. Eye protection is always needed when heating acids and solutions.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how a student removes excess copper oxide from copper sulfate solution.
Explain why this method removes the excess copper oxide but not the copper sulfate.

questions.explanation: Filter paper only holds back undissolved solid particles. Dissolved salt particles are small enough to pass through with the water.

questions.question:
A student heats copper sulfate solution strongly until all the water has gone.
Give two reasons why this is not a good idea.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: the hot solution may spit (hazard); the crystals may be damaged / decompose (lose water); produces a powder or small crystals rather than large crystals
questions.explanation: Evaporate only to the crystallisation point, then let the solution cool slowly. This is safer and gives larger, better-formed crystals.

questions.question:
Copper oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid.
Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.
Include state symbols.
markScheme: 1 mark: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O
1 mark: state symbols (s), (aq), (aq), (l)
questions.explanation: One of each substance balances. Copper oxide is a solid; the acid and salt are in solution; water is a liquid.

questions.question:
A student wants to make magnesium chloride crystals.
Name the acid the student should use.
Suggest a suitable insoluble magnesium compound.
markScheme: 1 mark: (dilute) hydrochloric acid
1 mark: magnesium oxide / magnesium carbonate / magnesium hydroxide (magnesium metal also accepted)
questions.explanation: Chlorides come from hydrochloric acid. Any insoluble magnesium compound that reacts with acid provides the magnesium ions.

questions.question:
Zinc chloride can be made from zinc carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.
Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.
Include state symbols.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae and balancing: ZnCO₃ + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
1 mark: state symbols (s), (aq), (aq), (l), (g)
questions.explanation: ZnCl₂ needs 2 Cl, so 2HCl. The 2 H form one H₂O and the carbonate gives CO₂.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows some of the apparatus used to make copper sulfate crystals.
Describe how to make pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

markScheme: Indicative content: measure about 40 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker; warm gently (about 50 °C) using a water bath or low Bunsen flame, do not boil; add copper oxide one spatula at a time, stirring; continue until copper oxide is in excess (black solid remains and no more dissolves); filter the mixture using filter paper and a funnel to remove excess copper oxide; collect the blue filtrate in an evaporating basin; heat gently over a water bath to evaporate some water until the crystallisation point (crystals form on a cold glass rod); leave to cool so crystals form; remove crystals (filter or pour off liquid) and pat dry with filter paper or leave in a warm place; wear eye protection.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method covering reacting with excess solid, filtering, crystallising and drying, with reasons (e.g. excess to use up all the acid).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most of the main steps in a sensible order, with some detail missing (e.g. no reason for excess or no drying step).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant steps, such as mixing copper oxide with acid or filtering, with little order.
questions.explanation: The four key stages are: react with excess solid, filter, crystallise and dry. Reasons such as 'excess so that all the acid reacts' help reach the top level.

questions.question:
A student made copper sulfate crystals.
The crystals were very small, felt damp and were mixed with some black powder.
Explain what went wrong in each case.
Suggest how to improve the method.
markScheme: Indicative content: black powder is unreacted copper oxide; filtering was not done carefully (filter paper torn, mixture poured over the top of the paper, or the step was skipped); improvement: filter carefully, possibly twice; very small crystals because the solution was evaporated too quickly or too far, or cooled too quickly; improvement: heat gently on a water bath only to the crystallisation point, then leave to cool slowly; damp crystals because they were not dried; improvement: pat dry between filter papers or leave in a warm place or desiccator.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains at least two of the problems with a correct cause and a suitable improvement for each.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies one problem or improvement with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: Each fault links to a stage: impurity to filtering, crystal size to evaporation and cooling rate, dampness to drying.

questions.question:
Table 1 gives information about two zinc compounds.
Plan how to make a pure, dry sample of zinc nitrate crystals.
In your answer you should:
• name the reactants
• explain the purpose of each step
• include a balanced symbol equation.
markScheme: Indicative content: reactants: dilute nitric acid and zinc carbonate; ZnCO₃(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g); warm the nitric acid gently to increase the rate; add zinc carbonate a spatula at a time with stirring; fizzing shows carbon dioxide is produced; keep adding until fizzing stops and white solid remains (excess) so all the acid has reacted; filter to remove the excess insoluble zinc carbonate; the filtrate is zinc nitrate solution; heat gently on a water bath to the crystallisation point; leave to cool to form crystals; separate and dry with filter paper; wear eye protection.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct reactants and equation, all stages in a logical order with the purpose of each step explained.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct reactants with most stages described; some purposes explained or equation partly correct.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one correct reactant or gives a few relevant steps with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use the information: zinc carbonate is insoluble, so excess can be filtered off; zinc nitrate is soluble, so it stays in the filtrate. Nitrates come from nitric acid.

questions.question:
A student heats copper sulfate solution to the crystallisation point.
The solution is then left to cool slowly.
Explain why crystals form as the solution cools.
Explain why cooling slowly is better than cooling quickly.
markScheme: 1 mark: the salt is less soluble at lower temperature, so crystals form as the solution cools
1 mark: slow cooling gives larger (better-formed) crystals
questions.explanation: A hot concentrated solution can hold more dissolved salt than a cold one. As it cools, the extra salt comes out of solution as crystals; slow cooling lets larger crystals grow.
